preview: An interview experience for a Morgan Stanley internship obtained through the Code to Give Hackathon, detailing the online assessment, hackathon phase, technical round, and HR round.
content: Morgan Stanley Interview Experience - Adwait Mandge (TY B.Tech - CS) Overview: Morgan Stanely did not visit our campus for both on-campus placements and internships. I was given a PPI (Pre-Placement-Interview) based on my performance in the Code to Give Hackathon held in June. Your performance in the hackathon is evaluated and based on it some students are offered either a PPO (Pre-Placement Offer) or a PPI. I was lucky to be one of the three students who were given a PPI. Online Assessment: The online assessment test for the Code To Give Hackathon was conducted on the 6th of May at 6:00pm. The test lasted for 2 hours and it had 3 sections. Aptitude, Debugging, Coding. The aptitude section consisted of 10 MCQs and we were given 20 minutes. I was not able to solve all the 10 questions and since there was no negative marking, I decided to attempt every question. The debugging section was relatively easier and mainly consisted of questions containing some syntactic and semantic errors. We were given 15 minutes to solve 7 debugging questions. I was able to do 6 but ran out of time. The coding round consisted of 3 questions. One question was based on level order traversal of binary tree and the other two were dynamic programming based. Question 1: In a family hierarchy, there are N family members. Each member has at most two children. Some members may have no children. Each member has a fixed annual income. The head of the family who is at the top of the hierarchy wants to know how much extra money would be required to make the total annual income of each generation of the family equal. Each level of the hierarchy is considered as a generation. The extra money is calculated as the positive value or 0 which should be added to the total income of each generation the same in all generations. The total income of a generation is the sum of income of all the members of the same generation. If a family is not earning then his income is denoted by -1 and this -1 will not get added in the total income of the generation. A simple level order traversal will do. I was able to clear all the test cases. I’m not able to recollect the other 2 questions but they were dynamic programming based questions. I could clear only half of the test cases in both these questions. The results of the OA were announced on the 19th of May and I was lucky to be one of the 7 students that had been shortlisted for the hackathon. Code to Give Hackathon: The hackathon officially commenced on the 2nd of June with a kick-off meet. We were assigned teams and mentors right before the meet itself. They gave us an overview of the hackathon, what was expected from our side, timeline, etc. After the meet, we had a team discussion and decided on the tech-stack that we were going to use and then we started developing our project the next day. We were required to give daily updates to the mentor regarding the project, what all things you had accomplished in the last 24 hours, what are the things that you plan on accomplishing in the next 24 hours and so on. Stay as active as you can on the discord server or whatever mode of communication you decide to use. This shows that you have immersed yourself in the project and ultimately generates an impression on the mentor as well. Ask for guidance wherever required, the mentors will always help you. On the final day of the hackathon, we were required to present our project to the jury. There were two rounds of evaluation. We were given 15 minutes for the presentation and had to demonstrate the prototype in those 15 minutes as well. Despite our best efforts, we couldn’t make it past the first round. Overall, it was an extremely enlightening experience. We received an update from Morgan Stanley regarding the status of PPIs and PPOs on the 24th of August. 1 student was offered a PPO and 3 were offered PPI. I was lucky to be one of the 3 students that were offered the PPI. Round 1 (Technical Round): The interview was held on the 1st of September at 12:00 pm. It lasted for about an hour. I joined the Zoom meeting 10 minutes prior and then was redirected to a breakout room where my interviewer arrived shortly afterwards. I was asked to introduce myself. You’ll be asked to introduce yourself in every interview round. Prepare a pretty solid introduction beforehand and mention some of the highlights of your resume in the introduction itself. I was then given a situation. Given a number of tasks (string) , what would be the data structure of your choice for storing these tasks? I first asked him if the number of tasks are fixed, to which he replied yes. Since we have a definite number of tasks with us, I said that I would use an array of strings for storing individual tasks. I was then told that there could be duplicate tasks present in the input, how would you keep track of the frequency of each task. I gave him two answers. First one being, instead of maintaining an array of strings, we could keep an array of pairs, where the first entity of the pair would represent the task and the second entity would represent its frequency. This would be disadvantageous as we would need to iterate through the entire array and find out if a particular task exists so as to increase its frequency along and there are several other drawbacks of having a fixed size array. To overcome this, we can use an unordered map and leverage its constant search time complexity to increase the frequency of tasks. He seemed satisfied with my answer and then we moved on to the next question. Given 10 teams numbered from 1 to 10, print the match schedule of all the teams such that the following conditions are satisfied. Only 1 match is scheduled in a day. No team is allowed to play on two consecutive days. If team A plays against team B on one particular day, they cannot play against each other on any other day. I verbally explained my approach. I was then asked to write the code. Basically, you need to keep a track of the teams that have already played against each other and the teams that have played on the previous day. To keep a track of the teams that have played on any given day, I used an unordered map where the integer key (day) is mapped to a pair representing the team that has played on that day. I used the set data structure where every element of the set was a vector of size 2 containing the teams that have played against each other (you can also use a 2D array of size 10x10 for this purpose). After finding a pair of teams that satisfies the given condition, map the current day to this pair, create a vector of size 2 and sort it and then finally store it in the set. Don’t stay silent for more than 7- 10 seconds, it creates a negative impact on the interviewer. Whatever you are writing in your text editor, simultaneously explain the logic to the interviewer. Drop comments wherever relevant, especially the code blocks that provide a critical insight into your code's functionality. I had inserted comments before loops, conditional statements and before performing any critical operation. As a result, when you are constantly adding and deleting lines of code while debugging, the interviewer will get a clear idea of the changes you make and their effects. Always ask clarifying questions to the interviewer, state all the aspects of the problem that you have understood and ask the interviewer to re-explain the parts that you haven’t understood. Always start-off by explaining the most natural approach towards the problem. Explain the drawbacks of the natural process and thereby state the techniques for eliminating the drawbacks. Unfortunately, the code did not give the desired output, I had dropped comments everywhere in my code to make it easier for the interviewer to understand what I had been doing. He gave me a hint and I made the best use of it but to no avail. I then provided a line by line explanation of the entire code and even highlighted the part of the code that should have taken care of the wrong output. I was then given 5 minutes to fix the code, I couldn’t think of anything at that point and started writing some redundant code. 5 minutes passed and then we moved on. Before moving on, he said that he only wanted to know my approach. I was made to choose between Databases and OOPs. I had a really strong grip on OOPs and hence chose OOPs. Right off the bat, he asked me to Design a Pen store. He didn’t want me to write the code, he just wanted to know how I would incorporate the pillars of Object Oriented Programming into designing a pen store. The interviewer provided a list of functions that should be included in the Pen Store class. It was a pretty easy question and I was able to give him a satisfactory explanation. He then asked me some pretty standard OOPs questions like, difference between Overloading and Overriding, what is a virtual function, etc. He then asked me if I had any questions for him. Always ask 1 or 2 questions to the interviewer, this shows that you are interested in the company. Shortly after the interview, I received a call and was told that I had been shortlisted for the HR Round. Round 2 (HR Round): The HR round started at 3:00 pm and lasted for 30 mins. The interviewer asked me to introduce myself, following which he asked me about one of my hackathon projects. I was told to explain the project. Always follow the STAR strategy for explaining projects. We had a discussion about this project for about 5 mins and then he asked some pretty standard HR questions and some situation based questions. As far as I’ve observed, they basically test your ability to gel with people, seamlessly work with teams, resolve conflicts and handle tight deadlines. He then asked me about my field of interest, what programming language I am currently learning, domains I would like to explore, etc . Since I had participated in several hackathons, I chose to respond to these questions within the context of hackathons. During hackathons, you are most likely to encounter situations that you’ll be given in your HR interview. This will demonstrate that you’ve been through similar situations and have always emerged with positive results. At the end of the interview, I was asked if I had any questions for him. Again, I asked him 2 questions and then the round ended. The results were announced late in the evening and I was lucky to be one of the candidates that had been offered the internship. Important Resources (Referred by me): Love Babbar 450 DSA Sheet, Love Babbar OOPs Sheet, JavaTPoint OOPs, VTable and Vpointers, Gate Smashers Operating Systems Playlist, Gate Smashers DBMS Playlist, Apna College DBMS Notes, Low Level Design, Interview Bit HR questions, Aptitude. Tips and Tricks: Prepare a good introduction and remember it by heart. Think out loud whatever you are thinking. Don’t make any assumptions, always ask the interviewer. Don’t mention projects in your resume that you haven’t worked on and if you don’t know a topic just let them know. Whenever the interviewer asks you a question, make sure that you understand the question correctly and I would suggest that you repeat whatever you understand again so that the interviewer can repeat the question again if you misunderstand something. Don’t get demotivated by rejections, analyze what went wrong and work on it. Try to understand things with real-world examples instead of mugging the definitions and try to remember an example for each topic you learn while preparing for CS-Fundamentals. Stay confident throughout the interview. Stay hydrated throughout the interview. If you’ve mentioned a group project on your resume, specify your contribution to the project. Believe in yourself and everything will fall in place.
